gameplay_summary: Single-screen platformer: climb girders and ladders as Mario, jump barrels and fireballs, and reach the top to rescue the Lady from Donkey Kong.
dossier: One of the Famicom's three launch games and Nintendo's home port of its 1981 arcade hit. You guide Mario (still unnamed in this era) up a construction site while Donkey Kong hurls barrels; jumping hazards scores points and the hammer lets you smash them for a few seconds. The cartridge has three stages rather than the arcade's four: the conveyor-belt factory stage was cut for space, along with the climbing intermissions and the height markers. The three stages loop with rising speed, so it is a score-attack game rather than one you finish. The port was considered remarkably close to the arcade for 1983. The NES cartridge is the same Nintendo port.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Pure arcade action with English on-screen text; nothing needs to be read to play.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Donkey Kong (North America 1986); both cartridges are the same Nintendo port.

gameplay_summary: Single-screen platformer: climb vines and chains as Donkey Kong Jr., dodge Mario's traps and drop fruit on enemies to reach the key and free Donkey Kong.
dossier: A Famicom launch title porting the 1982 arcade sequel, with the roles reversed: Mario is the jailer and you play Junior trying to free his father. The core trick is vine climbing: hold two vines to climb fast, one vine to slide down quickly. Snapjaws, birds and sparks patrol each screen, and knocking fruit off its perch wipes out anything beneath it. There are four stages, the last one pushing keys up to unlock the cage, and the game then loops at a higher difficulty. Unlike the Famicom Donkey Kong, this port kept all four arcade stages, losing only some small animations. The NES version is the same cartridge.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade action with English text; no Japanese is involved in normal play.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Donkey Kong Jr. (North America 1986); same Nintendo port in both regions.

gameplay_summary: Single-screen action game: move Popeye around a multi-level stage to catch the hearts, notes or letters Olive throws before they sink, while avoiding Brutus and the Sea Hag.
dossier: The third Famicom launch game, a port of Nintendo's 1982 arcade game based on the comic strip. Popeye cannot jump; he walks and climbs stairs and ladders between levels of the screen, punching away bottles and other thrown objects. Each of the three stages (dock, town, ship) has you collect everything Olive drops; miss one and it sinks, costing a life. Brutus chases you constantly and can only be beaten after eating the one can of spinach per stage, which briefly lets Popeye knock him into the sea. Stage gimmicks include a punching bag that can drop a bucket on Brutus. Clearing all three stages loops back to a harder first stage.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade action; the objectives are visual and need no reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Popeye (North America 1986).

gameplay_summary: Computer version of renju (tournament gomoku): take turns placing stones and be the first to make five in a row, against the computer or a second player.
dossier: A straight adaptation of renju, the competitive form of gomoku in which the first player (black) is barred from certain double threats and overlines so the game stays balanced. You play black against the computer at one of three levels or face a friend. Beginner flashes the opponent's open threes and fours as a hint (though not every danger), Intermediate removes the hints, and Advanced adds a 90-second move clock. Despite the box and title screen pushing the friendlier word gomoku, the rules are renju throughout. The content is nearly identical to Nichibutsu's 1981 arcade version. It was sold only in Japan, and nothing comparable came out on NES.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Only the difficulty menu is in Japanese (beginner, intermediate, advanced, two-player). Knowing renju's restrictions on black matters far more than reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Uses renju rules, so black (the player in one-player mode) loses to forbidden moves that plain gomoku would allow.

gameplay_summary: Two-player Japanese riichi mahjong against one computer opponent, played as a race to win three half-games (hanchan).
dossier: Nintendo's first Famicom mahjong game and one of the system's biggest early sellers, at over two million copies in Japan. Hardware limits cut the table to two players: you against one computer opponent, always seated as the first dealer. A half-game is four hands, and the first side to take three half-games wins the match. Riichi rules are used, with some quirks of the era, such as no closed pinfu-tsumo combination and a two-han minimum after a long repeat run. Three difficulty levels range from a tutorial-like mode that stops illegal mistakes to one with tight time limits on calls. There is no save. The four-player follow-up is 4 Nin Uchi Mahjong.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Play runs on tile graphics, but calls, yaku and scoring prompts appear in Japanese. Comfortable for someone who already knows riichi mahjong, hard for anyone learning it.
nes_counterpart_context: No North American release. Nintendo did sell the same game on NES in Hong Kong (1987); that cartridge is outside the North American NES set.

gameplay_summary: Single-screen platformer: bump turtles, crabs and flies from below to flip them, then kick them away, alone or with a second player as Luigi.
dossier: A port of the 1983 arcade game and the first proper Mario-and-Luigi game. Enemies pour out of the pipes, and you can't stomp them; you punch the floor beneath them to flip them over, then kick them off before they recover. Crabs take two hits and flies have to be caught when they land. The POW block stuns everything on screen, and coin-collecting bonus rounds appear every few phases. Two players share the screen at once, so it works co-operatively or as sabotage. The Famicom/NES cartridge shrinks some sprites and drops a few arcade details, notably the icicles. Two label variants exist, early pulse-line and later artwork labels.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade action with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Mario Bros. (North America 1986).

gameplay_summary: English-spelling game built on the Popeye engine: walk Popeye to letters to spell the English word for a Japanese prompt, or race a second player to collect falling letters.
dossier: Nintendo's first Famicom educational game, teaching English vocabulary to Japanese children with graphics reused from Famicom Popeye. In Word Puzzle A you get a word's meaning in katakana and must spell the English word by walking Popeye to the right letters. Every wrong letter costs points, and too many lets Brutus knock Swee'Pea's basket down. Word Puzzle B is the same with no Japanese hint, only the word length. Categories include animals, countries, food, sports and an oddly technical Science set. Word Catcher is a two-player race in which Popeye and Brutus grab drifting letters to finish a short word first. A printed word list came in the box. For an English speaker the spelling is trivial and the challenge is the Japanese.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — The main mode works by translating Japanese (katakana) prompts into English words, so it is pointless without reading them; Word Puzzle B can only be guessed from word lengths.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Nine-inning baseball against the computer or a friend: choose pitch speed and curve, time your swings, and throw to bases with the D-pad.
dossier: The Famicom's first baseball game, and the template many later Famicom baseball games followed, including mapping the four directions of the D-pad to the four bases. You pick one of six teams, which differ only in uniform colour, and play a full game of nine innings. Pitching lets you vary speed and steer the ball's path; batting is a timed swing; base-running and throws use the D-pad. Fielding is simple, with the computer doing much of the work. It is very bare by later standards, with no stats, seasons or player differences, but it was a huge seller in Japan. The NES release is the same game with American trappings.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Uses team initials and a standard scoreboard; no Japanese is needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Baseball (North America 1985).
japanese_version_notes: The six teams' initials match Japanese Central League clubs; the NES version swapped them for MLB-style initials. The Famicom version also shows the count in Japanese strike-ball-out order and pitch speed in km/h, which the NES changed to ball-strike order and mph.

gameplay_summary: Arithmetic game on the Donkey Kong Jr. engine: climb vines to collect numbers and operator signs that build an equation reaching Donkey Kong's target number.
dossier: Nintendo's second Famicom educational game after Popeye's English Fun, reusing Donkey Kong Jr.'s graphics and climbing. Donkey Kong holds up a target number, and Junior climbs vines and chains to grab digits and +, -, × and ÷ signs whose result must hit it. Calculate A and B work this way, against a rival player in two-player play, while +-×÷ Exercise gives fixed sums to solve. Mario is absent. Junior can only grip one vine here, so climbing is always slow and sliding fast. It is a children's math drill with a platformer skin, not a Donkey Kong game to play for fun; it famously flopped in North America.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Built entirely around numbers and arithmetic symbols; the in-game title reads さんすうあそび but nothing needs to be read.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Donkey Kong Jr. Math (1986); the title was changed but the game was not.

gameplay_summary: Tennis against the computer: time serves, normal shots and lobs in singles, or team up with a second player for doubles against two computer opponents.
dossier: Nintendo's first tennis game for the Famicom, with Mario as the umpire. Serving is a timed toss-and-swing (rushing the net gives a stronger serve), and in rallies you choose between normal shots and lobs. There are five computer skill levels, told apart by the opponent's uniform colour, with the ball getting faster at each. One player plays singles. Two players play doubles together against the computer; there is no head-to-head mode. Winning at higher levels shows an English victory message with a cup and prize money. The ball's shadow was praised at the time because it makes depth easy to read.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Sports action with English text; no reading is required.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Tennis (North America 1985).

gameplay_summary: Two-screen pinball table: keep the ball alive with the flippers on each screen, hit targets to light save features, and score as high as possible.
dossier: A simple two-screen pinball game by Nintendo and HAL. The view flips between the upper and lower halves of the table as the ball moves, and each half has its own flippers. Matching the slot machine, flipping all five cards or hatching three chicks raises posts and stoppers that guard the drains, which helps beginners. A bonus hole sends you to a Breakout-like bonus screen, where Mario bounces the ball into blocks to drop Pauline, and you need to catch her. Game B speeds up the ball, and two players alternate turns. There is no background music. The cartridge also includes copy protection that breaks the flippers if the game is run from RAM.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Pinball with no text to read.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Pinball (North America 1985).

gameplay_summary: Light-gun quick-draw game: wait for the outlaw's 'FIRE!!' signal, then shoot first; later modes pit you against two outlaws or a whole gang.
dossier: A light-gun Western duel adapted from Gunpei Yokoi's 1974 electro-mechanical arcade game, with cartoon sprites in place of the filmed footage. In Game A you face one gunslinger and must wait for his eyes to flash and the 'FIRE!!' bubble. Shooting early loses the duel, and you need to beat his draw time. Game B adds a second outlaw. Game C is a shootout against a gang in a building. The game is short and reflex-based, best in quick bursts. On Famicom it was sold for the 光線銃 (Kōsenjū) light gun series and needs that gun, a revolver styled after the Colt Single Action Army. The game is known for its cameo in Back to the Future Part II.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Reflex shooting with a visual cue; there is no text to read.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Wild Gunman (North America 1985).
japanese_version_notes: The Famicom game is played with the Kōsenjū light gun, which plugs into the Famicom's expansion port; an NES Zapper will not connect to a Famicom without an adapter.

gameplay_summary: Light-gun shooting: hit ducks (one or two at a time) or clay pigeons with three shots per target, meeting a quota each round to advance.
dossier: Nintendo's best-known light-gun game, first released on Famicom in 1984. Game A sends one duck at a time, Game B two, and Game C replaces the ducks with clay pigeons fired into the distance. You get three shots per target and ten targets per round, and you have to hit a rising minimum count to continue as the targets speed up. The hunting dog fetches your kills and laughs when you miss. It is simple and endless, built around high scores. It became the famous NES pack-in in North America. On Famicom it needs the Kōsenjū-series light gun.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Shooting game with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Duck Hunt (North America 1985).
japanese_version_notes: Requires a Famicom light gun (the Kōsenjū series), which plugs into the Famicom expansion port; the NES Zapper is not directly compatible.

gameplay_summary: Eighteen-hole golf: pick a club and aim, then time a three-stage swing meter for power and hook or slice, allowing for wind and hazards.
dossier: Nintendo and HAL's golf game, programmed by Satoru Iwata, and the best-selling sports game on Famicom/NES. One 18-hole course is played as stroke play, or as two-player stroke or match play. Each shot is club choice, aim, and a timed swing where you set power and then the curve. Wind, rough, water, bunkers and out-of-bounds trees make it a real game of golf despite the bare presentation. There is no music, only sound effects. The moustached golfer looks like Mario; Nintendo later named him Ossan in Captain Rainbow. A hidden copy of this game lived in early Nintendo Switch firmware as a tribute to Iwata.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Uses numbers and English labels; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Golf (North America 1985).
japanese_version_notes: The Famicom version measures distances in metres; overseas versions use yards.

gameplay_summary: Light-gun target range: three or five cardboard cutouts turn to face you, and you must shoot only the gangsters, quickly, without hitting civilians or police.
dossier: The third Famicom light-gun game, built like a police training range. Game A lines up three cutouts against a wall; when they turn, you shoot the gangsters and spare the innocents, against a reaction timer. Game B moves the cutouts onto a city street, where they slide in from cover in groups of five. Game C is a trick-shot mode: you keep tin cans in the air by shooting them and try to bounce them onto ledges. A wrong target or a slow shot costs you a miss. It is short and score-based, and the mix of good and bad targets makes it more of a decision test than Duck Hunt. It needs the Famicom Kōsenjū light gun.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Visual target-recognition game; there is no text to read.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Hogan's Alley (North America 1985).
japanese_version_notes: Requires a Famicom light gun (the Kōsenjū series), which plugs into the Famicom expansion port; the NES Zapper is not directly compatible.

gameplay_summary: Fixed-screen shooter: as exterminator Stanley, spray insecticide upward to drive Donkey Kong up his vines and stop bees from carrying off your flowers.
dossier: The third Donkey Kong game swaps platforming for shooting. Mario is gone, replaced by Stanley the bugman, who first appeared in a Game & Watch title. Donkey Kong hangs from vines in a greenhouse, and you push him to the top with bug spray or wipe out every insect to clear a stage. Bees try to steal the five flowers at the bottom, and a bee that gets one away powers up. One Super Spray can hangs on the vines per life and falls when Donkey Kong is pushed past it, giving a much stronger shot. Compared with the arcade, the Famicom version squashes the tall screen, starts with flowers in bloom, and makes running out of time an instant miss.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade shooting; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Donkey Kong 3 (North America 1986).

gameplay_summary: Puzzle-platformer: collect every gold pile on a stage of bricks, ladders and bars while dodging guards, digging holes to trap them, then climb out via the hidden ladder.
dossier: Hudson's port of Broderbund's Lode Runner, released alongside Nuts & Milk as the first third-party Famicom games. You can't attack; instead you burn holes in the brick floor on either side, either to drop to a lower level or to trap a chasing guard until the brick regrows. Guards also pick up gold, which has to be shaken loose from them. Once all the gold is taken, an escape ladder appears. Larger sprites than the Apple II original mean each level scrolls sideways. Each stage mixes route-planning puzzle and twitch evasion. There's an adjustable game speed, hidden fruit bonuses, and a stage editor. The guard robot sprite was later reused for Bomberman.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action-puzzle play with no text needed.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Lode Runner (1987), the same Hudson port published by Broderbund instead of Hudson.
japanese_version_notes: The stage editor can save custom levels to cassette with the Family BASIC data recorder, which the NES cartridge cannot use.

gameplay_summary: Single-screen platformer: as the blob Milk, collect all the fruit on a screen, then reach your girlfriend Yogurt before time runs out, dodging the rival Nuts.
dossier: Hudson's other day-one Famicom game, sold alongside Lode Runner, adapted from its own 1983 computer game; the Famicom version's content differs from the PC releases. Milk is the hero and Nuts is the enemy, despite the title order. Milk can't attack, only walk, climb ropes and jump, and his jump has an awkward arc, so this cute-looking pastel game is harder than it looks. Each screen asks you to grab every apple and banana, which opens Yogurt's house, then reach her without touching Nuts, blimps or the water. Every stage ending in 3 or 8 is a bonus run, out of fifty stages. There's an A/B difficulty choice and an editor for one custom stage.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action play with visual objectives; no text is needed.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. A Commodore 64 conversion of this version came out in the UK as Hot Pop! (1985).

gameplay_summary: Fixed-screen space shooter: slide your ship along the bottom and pick off a swaying alien formation as aliens peel off in curving dive attacks.
dossier: Namco's first Famicom game, a port of its 1979 arcade shooter. The aliens hover in formation and break off one or a few at a time in swooping attacks, firing as they dive. Flagships with escorts are worth big bonuses, and when only a few remain they all attack relentlessly. You get one shot on screen at a time, so timing and aim matter more than spraying. The port began as a test program Namco built while studying the Famicom hardware. It turned out good enough to sell, and it differs only slightly from the arcade in enemy movement. Late in the game, a hidden button-and-reset trick plays an unrelated melody.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade shooting with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; this Famicom port was released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Pac-Man-style maze game: as the dragon Tamagon, grab a cross to gain fire breath, eat the dots and roast monsters, while the Devil shifts the whole maze around you.
dossier: A Shigeru Miyamoto maze game built on Pac-Man ideas, with one big twist. The Devil dances at the top of the screen and points, and his minions crank the maze in that direction, so the walls scroll and can crush you against the edge. Tamagon is helpless until he touches a cross, which lets him breathe fire and eat dots. Holy imagery is central to the design, which is why Nintendo of America never released it. Two players can play simultaneously, co-operating or getting in each other's way. It's an early, very busy Nintendo arcade-style game, more chaotic than Pac-Man. It was released during Nintendo's price rise, so two box versions exist with identical contents.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade maze action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No North American release, because Nintendo of America's rules on religious imagery blocked it. It was released on NES in Europe (1987); that PAL cartridge is outside the North American NES set.
japanese_version_notes: This is the original version. The European release is essentially the same game; the UK version renames the Devil 'Demon'.

gameplay_summary: Maze chase: eat every dot while four ghosts hunt you, using power pellets to turn the tables and eat them for points.
dossier: Namco's Famicom port of the 1980 arcade classic, released under the western name Pac-Man rather than the original Japanese arcade title Puck-Man. You clear each maze of dots while Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde each chase you in their own pattern. The side tunnels slow the ghosts, and the four power pellets let you eat them for escalating points. Bonus fruit marks each level. The port is faithful for its time and even keeps the arcade's ghost-blindness quirk in certain spots. It is the version later used for Famicom Mini and Virtual Console releases.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade maze action with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Pac-Man, released in North America by Tengen (licensed 1988, then unlicensed 1989) and by Namco (1993).

gameplay_summary: Four-player Japanese riichi mahjong against three computer opponents, with a toggle to show the computer players' hands.
dossier: The four-player follow-up to Nintendo's two-player Famicom Mahjong, developed by Hudson Soft from its PC game Jan Kyou and published by Nintendo. It sold about 1.45 million copies in Japan. You play a standard four-handed riichi game against three computer opponents, choosing discards with left and right and calls with up and down. Pressing Select toggles an open mode that reveals the other hands, a feature inherited from the PC version, where it was meant to prove the computer wasn't cheating. The win screen shows at most seven yaku, though all are scored. Outside Japan the game is best known for its title screen, where the kanji 人 is drawn in a way many find phallic.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Commands (pon, chi, kan, riichi, ron, tsumo) and yaku appear in Japanese. Fine for a riichi player who recognises the terms, tough for a newcomer.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Behind-the-car racing in the style of Pole Position: weave through traffic and finish each course's laps within a time limit, shifting between low and high gear.
dossier: The Famicom's first racing game, from HAL with Satoru Iwata leading a small team. It was the first Famicom game to use raster scrolling for its pseudo-3D road. You drive a Formula One car with a two-speed gearbox, avoiding rival cars and staying on the track as the road curves. Crashes and run-offs slow or stop you, and the clock is what ends your game. Each of three difficulty levels is a run of courses; finishing a course's laps adds time and moves you on, and the final course of each level is an endless run until time expires. It is simple and fast but repetitive. A different Game Boy F1 Race came out in 1990.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Racing with English on-screen text; no reading is needed.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. The Game Boy F1 Race released overseas is a separate game.

gameplay_summary: Vertical-scrolling shooter: fly the Solvalou, using the Zapper on aircraft and aiming the Blaster's bomb sight at ground targets across 16 looping areas.
dossier: Namco's port of its 1983 arcade landmark; its arrival helped drive early Famicom sales. The hook is the two-weapon system: an air shot for flying enemies, and a bomb aimed with a reticle ahead of the ship for tanks, turrets and installations, which pushes you to read the ground as well as the sky. The 16 areas of forest, roads, rivers and Nazca-style lines loop endlessly, with Andor Genesis motherships as set-piece targets. Bombing invisible spots reveals hidden Sol towers and a Special Flag (an extra life). Much of the appeal is learning these secrets and the scoring.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade shooting with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Xevious, published in North America by Bandai (1988) rather than Namco.

gameplay_summary: Side-view street fight: trade high and low, weak and strong punches with a rival, guarding the right height, to push him off the edge of the screen and into a manhole.
dossier: Nintendo's first fighting game: a one-on-one street brawl on a city sidewalk. Each fighter blocks high or low, and you score by hitting the height your opponent isn't covering. Weak punches are fast but only nudge; strong punches knock down and shove the opponent back but leave you open. You can also dodge backward. Every punch drains stamina, and an exhausted fighter is reduced to feeble jabs. Push him off the screen edge three times and he drops down a manhole. Flower pots falling from windows add chaos, and these interruptions grow more frequent as the computer gets tougher. After 139 straight wins you earn the Champion title. It is very simple and was poorly regarded even at the time.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Fighting action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Urban Champion (North America 1986).

gameplay_summary: Single-screen action: as police mouse Mappy, bounce on trampolines between the floors of a cat gang's mansion and recover stolen goods while slamming doors on the cats.
dossier: Namco's port of its 1983 arcade game. The mansion is seen side-on: Mappy runs along each floor and uses the trampolines in the gaps to move between floors. A trampoline changes colour and breaks if you bounce on it too many times in a row. The Meowky cats and their boss Nyamco (Goro abroad) chase you. Doors are your weapon: open one in a cat's face to knock it back, and the flashing power doors release a wave that sweeps every cat it touches off the screen for big points. Recovering the stolen TVs, computers, paintings and safes clears a round, ideally in matching pairs for bonus points. Wait too long and a 'HURRY' warning speeds everything up. The bouncy music is a favourite of game composer Koichi Sugiyama.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade action with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; this Famicom port was released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Maze game where your character never stops swimming: grab turning posts to swing around them, uncover the hidden gold ingots by passing between posts, and avoid the sea-urchin enemies.
dossier: A strange early Nintendo game built on awkward controls on purpose. Gloopy (Bubbles in English) moves forward constantly, and you steer only by reaching out an arm to grab a post and swing around it, or by bouncing off walls. Passing between two posts may reveal a hidden gold ingot, and each stage's ingots form a picture such as a heart or mushroom. Some gaps hide rubber traps that bounce you back and seal that route. The Unira enemies can be stunned with a sound wave and then crushed against a wall; black holes are deadly unless you swing over them. From stage 22 onward, passing back over a revealed ingot flips it face-down, adding a puzzle layer. Two players can play simultaneously.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action-puzzle play with no text to read.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Clu Clu Land (North America 1985).

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling motocross: race against the clock or computer riders, using turbo without overheating, changing lanes, and angling the bike to land jumps cleanly.
dossier: Shigeru Miyamoto's side-view motocross game, whose smooth-scrolling engine fed directly into Super Mario Bros. You race on four lanes: the A button is normal throttle, while B is a faster turbo that heats the engine until it overheats and stalls you. Cooling arrows on the track reset the temperature. Ramps and bumps are the real challenge, because you have to tilt the bike to match the slope or you crash on landing. Selection A is a solo time trial; Selection B adds computer riders you can knock over by cutting in front of them. Finish third or better in a preliminary race to enter the Excitebike race on each of five tracks. Design mode lets you build your own tracks from obstacle pieces.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Racing with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Excitebike (North America 1985).
japanese_version_notes: Design-mode tracks can be saved to cassette with the Family BASIC data recorder; the NES cartridge has no way to save them.

gameplay_summary: Joust-style action: flap to fly, pop enemy balloons by hitting them from above, and finish off fallen enemies before they re-inflate; plus an endless side-scrolling Balloon Trip mode.
dossier: Nintendo and HAL's take on Joust. You float with two balloons, tapping or holding a button to flap with real momentum. Hit an enemy from above and its balloon pops; it parachutes down and starts pumping up a new one, unless you knock it out first. Losing one balloon makes you sluggish, and losing both, touching lightning, or the giant fish in the water costs a life. Bonus stages have you grab balloons floating up from pipes. Two players can co-operate or, more often, sabotage each other. The Famicom version added Balloon Trip, which is not in the arcade game: an endless scrolling run dodging sparks and popping balloons. Some players buy the cartridge just for that mode.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade action with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Balloon Fight (North America 1986).

gameplay_summary: Vertical platformer: break through layers of ice with a mallet to climb a mountain, avoiding creatures that patch the holes, then race up a bonus stage to grab vegetables and the condor.
dossier: Popo and Nana (the second player) climb each of 32 mountains by smashing the ice above their heads and jumping through. Each mountain is eight floors. Topi creatures push ice blocks back into the gaps you make, birds swoop, and polar bears shake the screen. Some blocks are unbreakable, some floors slide like conveyor belts, and moving clouds act as platforms. The bonus stage at the summit is a timed climb for vegetables, ending with a jump to catch the condor. The jumping physics are stiff, with no steering in mid-air, which defines the challenge. Two players can co-operate or compete, and the stage select makes it a good head-to-head game.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Platform action; nothing needs reading.

dossier: The game that established Bomberman, a Hudson remake of its 1983 computer game Bakudan Otoko. Each stage is a grid of indestructible pillars and breakable blocks. dossier: Capcom's 1985 arcade shooter (Savage Bees in North America), published on Famicom by Tokuma Shoten. Capcom's yearly limit on Famicom releases pushed it to another publisher. gameplay_summary: Ball-routing puzzle: move two linked arrow cursors around a 4x4 grid of rooms and swap their contents, steering cascades of balls down into the highest-scoring trays.
dossier: Irem's 1985 arcade puzzle game, which began as a magazine type-in program. Tokuma Shoten published the Famicom version, developed by HAL. You steer a red arrow; a green arrow follows it a few seconds behind, and pressing the button swaps the contents of the two rooms they point at.
